w: What's tested The drug names in each class, especially the ones he highlighted in red What 5-alpha-reductase and aromatase do to testosterone, and the drugs that block them Blood clots: the biggest risk of estrogens, shared by the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors The three ways to block androgens Tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for bone, Clomid for ovulation Testosterone's liver risk, and Plan B versus ulipristal Dr. Fasinu's drug lecture on the sex hormones: androgens and the drugs that block them, estrogens and the drugs that block them, then progestins and anti-progestins. He said to focus on the drugs he highlighted on his slides. These notes follow the recording and slides. Which hormone to avoid Avoid testosterone with an enlarged prostate (BPH), in pregnancy and in a man with breast cancer. Avoid estrogen with breast cancer and in anyone who has had a blood clot. Clots are estrogen's worst and most common side effect. Making the hormones Cholesterol becomes DHEA, then androstenedione, then testosterone. DHEA is sold over the counter as a supplement, and older men take it for "andropause." Every other testosterone product is a controlled drug (Schedule III). His slide's table calls DHEA "dihydrotestosterone"; he corrected it: DHEA is dehydroepiandrosterone, and DHT is dihydrotestosterone. Testosterone then goes one of two ways. 5-alpha-reductase turns it into DHT, the active form. Aromatase turns it into estradiol. Block the first and you lower androgen activity; block the second and you lower estrogen. DHT makes you grow; estradiol stops growth by closing the growth plates. A man with no aromatase has no estradiol, so he grows very tall with weak, thin bones. Testosterone The hypothalamus sends GnRH in pulses, the pituitary answers with LH and FSH, and the testes make testosterone. Testosterone makes more red blood cells, holds on to salt and water (bad for high blood pressure), lowers good cholesterol (HDL), builds muscle, and lowers the proteins that carry hormones in the blood. Like all steroid hormones, it rides a carrier (SHBG), gets into the cell and works on the genes, so it is slow. Drugs: testosterone itself (gel, patch, nasal gel, injection) and testosterone cypionate, the shot into the muscle that lasts for weeks. Know those two; he didn't want to bother you with the others on his table. Uses: low testosterone in men, anemia that won't respond to other treatment, muscle wasting, and aging men. Side effects are worse in women and children. Women grow facial hair and get a deep voice, an enlarged clitoris and smaller breasts, sometimes for good. Men can get sleep apnea, a painful lasting erection (priapism) and breast growth, probably because some testosterone turns into estradiol. The one he said to remember: liver damage. No testosterone with liver disease or in pregnancy. Put the gel on at bedtime so you don't pass it to a child by hugging. Blocking androgens: three ways GnRH analogs (goserelin, sold as Zoladex; leuprolide): natural GnRH comes in pulses. A long-acting copy that never stops switches the pituitary off, so testosterone falls. Used for prostate cancer, BPH, early puberty and chemical castration. Side effects: impotence and breast growth. 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride): they stop testosterone from becoming DHT. Proscar and Propecia are both finasteride: the bigger dose for BPH, the smaller one for hair loss. Side effects: breast growth and sexual problems. Androgen receptor blockers (flutamide, bicalutamide): they sit on the androgen receptor. Used for prostate cancer, and for too much androgen in women. Side effects: stomach upset (least with bicalutamide), breast growth and liver damage. Estrogens There are three natural ones: estradiol from the ovary, and estrone and estriol from the liver and other tissues. Estrone and estriol leave in the bile and come back from the gut. Estrogen taken by mouth hits the liver hardest. Estrogen builds the female body and the uterine lining, raises good cholesterol (and triglycerides), protects bone and keeps skin healthy (some teens get the pill for their skin). It also makes the liver produce more clotting factors (2, 7, 9 and 10) and less antithrombin III. That is why estrogens, and even the anti-estrogens, cause clots. Drugs: estradiol (patch, gel, shot); ethinyl estradiol, the one in birth control pills; and estrone, the main part of Premarin, for menopause. Uses: low estrogen, menopause, birth control, very painful periods or excess hair, and fertility. Side effects: nausea, fluid retention (an androgen problem too; it raises blood pressure), breakthrough bleeding and sore breasts; and the serious ones, clots, uterine and breast cancer, and high blood pressure. Adding progesterone protects the uterus. No estrogen in pregnancy, in someone still growing, with unexplained genital bleeding, after any clot or stroke (even 10 years ago), with heart disease, or with a family history of breast or uterine cancer. Estrogen also makes blood thinners like warfarin work less well. SERMs Estrogen has two receptors, alpha and beta, and each tissue has its own mix. So one drug can act like estrogen in one tissue and block it in another. Tamoxifen: blocks estrogen in the breast and turns it on in the uterus. For breast cancer, but only when the tumor has estrogen receptors. Risks: uterine cancer and clots. Raloxifene (Evista): for bone loss after menopause. It doesn't stimulate the uterus or the breast. Clot risk is 2 to 3 times higher. Clomiphene (Clomid): blocks estrogen's brake on the brain, so LH and FSH surge and the ovary releases eggs. A fertility drug; twins and triplets are common. His short version: tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for osteoporosis, Clomid for ovulation. Aromatase inhibitors Anastrozole (Arimidex) stops testosterone from becoming estradiol, to treat breast cancer. Remember hot flashes and clots. Not for women before menopause or with liver damage. Progesterone and progestins Progesterone matures the uterine lining. Progestin drugs act on its receptor and hold down FSH, so no egg is released. Women who can't take estrogen (a clot, or breast or uterine cancer) use progestin-only birth control. Levonorgestrel is the common one, and Plan B is a big dose of it. Side effects: high blood pressure and lower HDL. His cases Least estrogen-like of four hormones: levonorgestrel, a progestin. A man on finasteride for hair loss with a low sex drive and sore breasts: the drug blocks 5-alpha-reductase. A woman on raloxifene whose extraction site heals slowly: watch for a clot while she's laid up. Emergency contraception Plan B (levonorgestrel) works within 72 hours and needs no prescription. Ulipristal (Ella) blocks the progesterone receptor, works up to 5 days, and needs a prescription. Mifepristone also blocks cortisol's receptor, so it is not for someone with Addison disease.
